questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer presents with painless ulcer on the hand with surrounding satellite lesions, regional lymphadenopathy and black eschar. Gram stain shows large Gram-positive rods in chains. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax presents with a painless ulcer with black eschar (malignant pustule), surrounding oedema, and satellite vesicles. The causative organism Bacillus anthracis appears as large Gram-positive rods in chains on smear. Farmers, veterinarians, and wool handlers are at risk.

questions.q: A 28-year-old sexually active male presents with painful genital ulcer with ragged undermined edges and tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. Smear shows Gram-negative rods arranged in school-of-fish pattern. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chancroid is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a Gram-negative bacillus. It presents with a painful genital ulcer with ragged undermined edges (unlike syphilis which is painless). Smear shows the classic school-of-fish or railroad-track pattern. Painful inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo) is characteristic.

questions.q: A 45-year-old immunocompetent patient presents with chronic verrucous plaques on the lower extremities with 'cauliflower-like' surface. KOH mount shows brown sclerotic bodies with cross-wall septation (Medlar bodies). What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis presents with verrucous, cauliflower-like plaques, typically on the lower limbs. Medlar bodies (also called copper pennies or sclerotic bodies) — pigmented thick-walled round cells with cross-wall septation — are pathognomonic on histology or KOH mount. Common causative fungi include Fonsecaea pedrosoi and Cladophialophora carrionii.

questions.q: A 30-year-old leprosy patient on MDT develops sudden painful swelling of pre-existing skin lesions, new erythematous painful nodules on the extensor surface, and fever. Nerve function is intact. What is this reaction?
questions.exp: Erythema Nodosum Leprosum (ENL) — Type 2 lepra reaction — occurs predominantly in lepromatous and borderline lepromatous leprosy. It presents as painful erythematous nodules, fever, and systemic features. It is an immune complex-mediated (Type III hypersensitivity) reaction. Unlike Type 1 (reversal), ENL involves extensor surface crops and systemic involvement.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, malar rash sparing nasolabial folds, discoid plaques, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive. Which antibody, if positive, would be most specific for this diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Sm (anti-Smith) antibody is the most specific antibody for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), though not the most sensitive. Anti-dsDNA is also specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity/nephritis. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and Sjogren's syndrome. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male presents with tense bullae on normal and erythematous skin, predominantly on the inner thighs, flexures, and abdomen. Nikolsky sign is negative. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at dermoepidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is characterized by tense bullae (subepidermal blister), negative Nikolsky sign, predominantly flexural distribution in elderly patients. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 deposition along the BMZ. The target antigens are BP180 (collagen XVII) and BP230 (BPAG1). It is the most common autoimmune blistering disease.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman on long-term hydroxychloroquine for RA develops yellowish-brown discolouration of her shins and blue-grey pigmentation in sun-exposed areas. What is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine (and chloroquine) can cause bluish-grey pigmentation in sun-exposed areas and yellowish discolouration in pretibial regions due to deposition of drug-melanin complexes. Minocycline causes blue-grey pigmentation in scars and shins. Amiodarone causes blue-grey photoexposed pigmentation with corneal microdeposits.

questions.q: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base in a dermatomal distribution on the trunk, not crossing the midline. Which antiviral is most appropriate?
questions.exp: Herpes zoster in an immunocompromised host should be treated with valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days (higher bioavailability than acyclovir) or famciclovir 500 mg TDS for 7 days. Acyclovir 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days is the alternative. Ganciclovir IV is reserved for CMV. The higher dose and longer duration reflect immunocompromised status.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with a slowly enlarging painless solitary nodule on the dorsum of the hand following a prick injury in the garden. The nodule has developed a central ulcer and satellite nodules tracking up the lymphatics of the forearm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii) classically presents with the sporotrichoid spread pattern — a primary inoculation nodule with subsequent satellite nodules tracking along lymphatics. It follows traumatic inoculation (rose-thorn, wood splinters). Diagnosis is confirmed by culture. Treatment is with itraconazole or potassium iodide (SSKI).

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with scaly annular patches with central clearing and broken hair stubs in the scalp. KOH shows ectothrix pattern and Wood's lamp shows bright green fluorescence. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Microsporum canis causes tinea capitis with ectothrix pattern (spores outside hair shaft) and fluoresces bright green under Wood's lamp (due to pteridine production). Trichophyton tonsurans and T. violaceum cause endothrix pattern without fluorescence. Epidermophyton floccosum does not infect hair.

questions.q: During a leprosy survey, a child has a single hypopigmented macule with definite loss of sensation on the buttock. Slit-skin smear is negative. This is classified as:
questions.exp: According to WHO operational classification, a patient with a single skin lesion with definite loss of sensation and negative SSS is classified as single-lesion paucibacillary (SLPB) leprosy. This is treated with ROM (Rifampicin + Ofloxacin + Minocycline) single dose. BT has 2-5 lesions; TT has 1-2 lesions but with well-defined borders; indeterminate has no definite sensory loss.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with violaceous flat-topped papules on the wrists and ankles with Wickham's striae visible on dermoscopy. There is also involvement of the buccal mucosa with white lacy pattern. What is the first-line systemic treatment?
questions.exp: Lichen planus with mucosal involvement and widespread cutaneous disease requires systemic therapy. Oral prednisolone (0.5-1 mg/kg/day) is the first-line systemic treatment for generalized lichen planus. It provides rapid symptom relief. Topical steroids and tacrolimus are used for limited disease. Dapsone has a role in bullous LP.

questions.q: A 65-year-old farmer presents with a slowly growing, non-tender, indurated plaque on the lower lip with surface crusting and an irregular margin. Biopsy shows islands of atypical keratinocytes with keratin pearls invading the dermis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lower lip in an elderly farmer is a classic presentation of chronic actinic damage. Histology shows invasive nests of atypical keratinocytes with keratin pearl formation and individual cell keratinization. SCC of lip carries higher metastatic risk (~10%) than cutaneous SCC. Risk factors include UV exposure, smoking, and immunosuppression.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with a pigmented lesion on the sole that has an irregular border. Dermoscopy shows a parallel ridge pattern. What does this finding suggest?
questions.exp: In acral dermoscopy, a parallel ridge pattern (pigment on the ridges/furrows running along the fingerprint ridges) is the key dermoscopic sign of acral lentiginous melanoma. In contrast, benign acral naevi show a parallel furrow pattern (pigment in the sulci). The parallel ridge pattern has high sensitivity (86%) and specificity (99%) for melanoma.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with psoriasis is planning pregnancy. Which antipsoriatic drug is absolutely contraindicated and requires a 3-year washout period before conception?
questions.exp: Acitretin (retinoid) is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category X) and requires a 3-year washout period due to its storage in adipose tissue and conversion to etretinate in the presence of alcohol. Methotrexate requires a 3-6 month washout. Cyclosporine has been used in pregnancy but is not first choice. Apremilast data is limited; generally avoided.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with sudden onset painful palpable purpura on the lower legs, arthritis, haematuria, and abdominal pain following an upper respiratory tract infection. Skin biopsy shows IgA deposits in vessel walls. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (HSP) presents with the classic tetrad: palpable purpura (non-thrombocytopenic), arthritis/arthralgia, abdominal pain/GI involvement, and renal disease (haematuria/proteinuria). It commonly follows an URTI. Pathognomonic finding is IgA deposition in small vessel walls on DIF. It is the most common systemic vasculitis in children but can occur in adults.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with severe pruritus after sun exposure, with urticarial wheals appearing within minutes of sun exposure and resolving within 24 hours without pigmentation. Phototesting shows urticarial response to UVA. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Solar urticaria presents with immediate urticarial wheals (within minutes) on sun-exposed skin that resolve within 24 hours without pigmentation. It is a Type I (IgE-mediated) or photoallergic reaction. Phototesting with various wavelengths identifies the action spectrum (often UVA or visible light). Polymorphous light eruption occurs hours to days later with papules/vesicles.

questions.q: A patient presents with diffuse hair loss 3 months after a major surgery. Pull test is positive with club-shaped (telogen) hair roots. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Telogen effluvium (TE) is characterized by diffuse hair shedding 2-3 months after a trigger event (surgery, illness, childbirth, stress, thyroid disease). Positive pull test with club-shaped telogen roots (no anagen bullb). Anagen effluvium occurs within weeks of chemotherapy and shows tapered fracture. Alopecia areata is patchy with exclamation-mark hairs.

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with yellow discolouration of all nails with slow growth, increased transverse curvature, and absence of lunula. He has a history of recurrent pleural effusions. What is this nail finding called?
questions.exp: Yellow nail syndrome is characterized by the triad of yellow slow-growing nails (with increased curvature and absent lunula), lymphoedema, and respiratory manifestations (pleural effusions, bronchiectasis, sinusitis). It is associated with lymphatic dysfunction. Treatment includes vitamin E, antifungals (if superinfection), and management of underlying condition.

questions.q: A 70-year-old presents with a pearly, translucent papule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the nose that has been slowly growing over years. It has a central ulceration. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) on the nose — a high-risk H-zone area — is best treated with Mohs micrographic surgery, which provides the highest cure rate (99%) and maximum tissue sparing by real-time margin assessment. Standard excision is appropriate for low-risk truncal BCC. Cryotherapy and imiquimod are for superficial BCC only.

questions.q: A 22-year-old with severe nodulocystic acne is being started on isotretinoin. Which of the following is a mandatory baseline investigation before starting therapy?
questions.exp: Before starting isotretinoin, a fasting lipid profile (triglycerides and cholesterol) is mandatory as isotretinoin commonly causes hypertriglyceridaemia and hypercholesterolaemia, which can rarely lead to pancreatitis. Liver function tests and a urine pregnancy test (in females) are also required. Blood counts may be monitored but lipids are the key mandatory baseline.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man with genital ulcers develops painful inguinal lymphadenopathy that forms bubo with 'groove sign'. PCR is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. What are the causative serovars?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3. The groove sign (Greenblatt's sign) — a groove between enlarged nodes above and below the inguinal ligament — is characteristic. Serovars A-C cause trachoma; D-K cause non-gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.

questions.q: A 25-year-old athlete presents with well-defined scaly patches in the groin with central clearing and peripheral scaling. The scrotum is spared. KOH shows fungal hyphae. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Tinea cruris (jock itch) with scrotal sparing is characteristic of Epidermophyton floccosum, which cannot infect hair. Trichophyton rubrum is the most common cause overall (may involve scrotum). Candida intertrigo typically involves the scrotum and satellite lesions are present. E. floccosum produces only macroconidia (no microconidia) and does not fluoresce.

questions.q: A patient with scleroderma develops fixed digital pitting scars on fingertips, telangiectasia, and calcinosis cutis. ANA shows a centromere pattern. What is the antibody associated with this finding?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibody (ACA) is strongly associated with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc) / CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia). Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-RNA polymerase III is associated with diffuse SSc and renal crisis.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman presents with pruritic grouped vesicles on elbows, knees, and buttocks. Small bowel biopsy shows villous atrophy. DIF of perilesional skin shows granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. DIF shows pathognomonic granular IgA in dermal papillae (unlike linear IgA disease). Dapsone provides rapid and dramatic itch relief within 48-72 hours and is the treatment of choice for skin lesions. Gluten-free diet is the definitive long-term treatment that can eventually allow dapsone discontinuation.

questions.q: A 50-year-old presents with recurrent episodes of blistering on sun-exposed skin (hands, face) with scarring and milia formation. Urine turns pink-red on standing and shows coral-pink fluorescence under Wood's lamp. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) presents with photosensitivity, skin fragility, blisters on sun-exposed areas, scarring, milia, hypertrichosis, and hyperpigmentation. Urine shows high uroporphyrins causing pink-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp. It is the most common porphyria. Triggers include alcohol, oestrogens, iron overload, and hepatitis C. Treatment includes phlebotomy and low-dose chloroquine.

questions.q: During patch testing, a patient shows a reaction of vesicles beyond the test site and intense erythema at 48 and 96 hours. This grade of patch test reaction is recorded as:
questions.exp: The ICDRG (International Contact Dermatitis Research Group) grading: – (negative), ?(doubtful/macular erythema), + (weak: erythema, oedema), ++ (strong: vesicles, erythema, infiltration), +++ (extreme: bullae, spreading beyond test site). Vesicles beyond the test site and intense erythema represents an extreme (+++) reaction. Irritant reactions lack vesicles and typically fade early.

questions.q: A 24-year-old presents with salmon-pink plaques with silvery-white scales on the scalp, elbows, and knees. Nail examination shows proximal pitting and onycholysis. Auspitz sign is positive. Which histopathological finding is most specific for this condition?
questions.exp: Munro microabscesses (collections of neutrophils in the parakeratotic stratum corneum) are the most specific histopathological finding in psoriasis. Spongiform pustules of Kogoj in the spinous layer are also characteristic. Civatte bodies (eosinophilic colloid bodies) are seen in lichen planus. Corps ronds and grains are seen in Darier disease.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with hyperpigmented macules on the cheeks, upper lip, and forehead with a reticulate pattern, worsening in summer. She is on oral contraceptives. What is the most effective topical treatment?
questions.exp: Kligman's formula (modified triple combination: hydroquinone 4% + tretinoin 0.025-0.05% + fluocinolone acetonide 0.01%) is the gold standard for melasma treatment. It works synergistically: HQ inhibits melanogenesis, tretinoin promotes skin turnover, and steroid reduces irritation. Sun protection is mandatory. OCP-induced melasma may resolve after stopping OCP.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man with a history of extensive sun exposure presents with multiple ill-defined erythematous scaly patches on the scalp and face that are tender to touch. Histology shows atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis with preservation of the basement membrane. What is the diagnosis and best treatment?
questions.exp: Actinic keratosis (solar keratosis) presents as scaly erythematous patches in sun-damaged skin. Histology shows full-thickness or partial-thickness epidermal atypia without basement membrane breach (carcinoma in situ equivalent). 5-FU cream is effective for field therapy treating multiple lesions. Other options include imiquimod, diclofenac, cryotherapy for isolated lesions, and PDT. Bowen's disease is full-thickness SCC in situ.

questions.q: A dermatology resident is performing dermoscopy of a nail. They observe a triangular or trapezoidal arrangement of longitudinal brown lines that are wider at the proximal nail fold and narrower at the free edge. What does this pattern indicate?
opts: Benign nail matrix naevus in adults
questions.exp: The 'micro-Hutchinson sign' or a band widening proximally with lines of irregular colour and spacing in nail dermoscopy (especially in adults) is highly suspicious for subungual melanoma. The 'triangle sign' — a band wider at the cuticle (proximal) than the free edge — is a red flag for ungual melanoma. Benign melanonychia shows parallel lines of uniform colour and spacing.
